parts.title: The name, and the house on the hill
parts.intro: D'Arcy was coined twice over, once in Normandy as the name of a place and once in Ireland as the name of a colour. The family tree runs the line back to a Yorkshire castle and an earldom and on to the kings of Denmark; this archive reaches a Gloucestershire yeoman in 1654. These pages set out the name, the two grafts it does not accept, the DNA that was its first check from outside the paper record, and the places its people can be put.

parts.title: An engineer at Chatham, a major of the 39th
parts.intro: Fifteen generations are asserted on the direct line and six of them this archive will defend. The documented line runs from Robert D'Arcy, commissioned in the Royal Engineers in 1776 and buried at Chatham in 1827, through his marriage and children at Portsea and Chatham, to a major of the 39th Foot. These pages follow the spine, the chart, the generations the tree never held, and the household.

parts.title: Gloucestershire and Bristol
parts.intro: The archive's oldest claim is a Gloucestershire yeoman born in 1654. The line it called untestable is tested here against the registers at Berkeley, the hamlet the name comes off, and a muster of 1608; beside it are the Wakefields, a mason from Stroud who married a Berkeley woman in Bristol, the 1841 census page that holds the family, and two pages kept as wrong.

parts.title: The Potteries and the Sneyds
parts.intro: Every Staffordshire Sneyd record, assembled into households, produces the family the tree had been pointing at. The Keele descent, followed into the registers, was found to be wrong. The Sneyds then go out of Bristol and Kempsey into far western Queensland, married at Muttaburra and born at Boulia, and a Hanley grocer's son sails for New South Wales in 1832.

parts.title: The crossing, and Brisbane
parts.intro: Seven lines reached Australia seven different ways: a garrison posting, a convict ship, a free passage, a paid one, and three nobody has dated. A major of the 39th Foot reached Port Jackson in September 1826 on the convict ship England, with his wife and baby daughter in the cabin, and the General Hewitt followed in 1854. These pages run on to Brisbane, an inquest in 1902, the Great War and the graves.

parts.title: The families they married, and how the lines join
parts.intro: A D'Arcy married a Sneyd, who was the granddaughter of a Wakefield of Bristol, and the line the archive is named for is one thread of thirteen families, out of Limerick, Monaghan, Cork, Ayrshire, Lanarkshire, Somerset, Bristol, London and Germany. These pages give each family, the marriages in date order, the women, the blood relatives, and how this archive joins the others.

parts.title: How we know
parts.intro: Every claim on this site carries its confidence. The sources are counted and sorted into records and other people's trees; every source read and found empty is published; and the indexes, the open questions, the errands, the corrections and the work list say what is not yet known. The investigations at the end read the archive against itself.
